name: Divide and Conquer and the Master Theorem
intent: Predict the cost of a divide-and-conquer algorithm by adding up the work at each level of its recursion tree, use the master theorem as a shortcut for that sum, and see when splitting does not help, when an uneven split breaks the saving, and how much of the work can run in parallel.
scenario: Merge sort on 1,000 numbers takes 18,717 counted operations (comparisons plus copies) and recurses 11 levels deep. Splitting the list 10% and 90% instead of in half raises that to 38,125; peeling off one element at a time raises it to 757,941 at a depth of 1,000, worse than insertion sort at 513,893. Then the team runs the sort on 64 workers and finds that the final merge, which runs alone, caps the speed-up near 10.
problem: Divide and conquer (split the problem, solve the parts, combine the answers) gives merge sort, binary search, fast matrix multiplication and many others, and it is easy to believe that splitting is itself the saving. It is not: splitting only helps when the pieces are small enough, balanced enough and cheap enough to combine. To judge a recursive algorithm you need to count the work of the whole recursion tree, and that is what the master theorem automates for the common shape T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n).

howItWorks.title: Split, solve, combine, and read the recursion tree
howItWorks.text: Merge sort splits a list in two, sorts each half the same way, and merges the sorted halves. Draw the calls as a tree: the root is the whole list, its children the two halves, and so on down to single elements. Each level handles all n elements once in total, in merges, so every level costs about the same, and the tree has about log2 n levels. For 1,000 numbers that is 8,741 comparisons plus 9,976 copies, 18,717 operations over 11 levels, about two operations per element per level, which is n log n growth. The same list through insertion sort, which does not divide, costs 513,893.

howItWorks.title: The master theorem is 'which level dominates'
howItWorks.text: For T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n): there are a to the power k sub-problems at level k, each of size n over b to the power k. Compare the cost of the leaves (about n to the power log base b of a) with f(n), the cost of combining at the top. If the leaves are bigger, they dominate and the total is the leaf count (tree sum: 2,047 for 1,024 elements, linear). If f(n) is bigger, the root dominates and the total is about f(n) (a combine step costing n squared gives 2,096,128 against 1,048,576 at the root). If they tie, every level costs the same and the total is f(n) times the number of levels (merge sort: 11,264 for 1,024 elements). Binary search ties too, with f = 1: 11 steps.

howItWorks.title: Uneven splits: a fixed fraction survives, a fixed count does not
howItWorks.text: What matters is how deep the tree gets. Splitting 25% and 75% still shrinks every piece by a constant factor, so the depth stays logarithmic (25 levels instead of 11 for 1,000 elements) and the cost is still n log n with a larger constant: 23,121 operations. At 10% and 90% the depth is 59 and the cost 38,125. But peeling off one element at a time is not dividing the problem at all: the depth is n and the cost grows as n squared (757,941, about three quarters of n squared with comparisons and copies counted), and the recursion needs 1,000 stack frames. A quicksort with a consistently bad pivot degenerates in exactly this way.

howItWorks.title: When splitting does not help
howItWorks.text: Three situations waste the split. The combine step is too costly: with f(n) equal to n squared the root level costs half the total, and a plain nested loop would do as well. The pieces are not much smaller than the whole, as in peeling one element. Or the pieces overlap, so the same sub-problem is solved again and again, which is a case for memoization, not for splitting. Adding sub-problems also hurts fast: eight sub-problems of half the size with an n-squared combine (naive block matrix multiply) cost 2,146,435,072 at n = 1,024, and seven (Strassen's rearrangement) cost 657,710,813. One fewer sub-problem changes the exponent, not just the constant.

howItWorks.title: Parallel potential: work against span
howItWorks.text: The halves of a divide-and-conquer algorithm are independent, so they can run on different workers. Total work is the sum over the whole tree; the span is the longest chain of steps that must happen one after another. In merge sort with a sequential merge, the final merge touches every element on its own, so for 2 to the power 20 elements the work is 22,020,096 but the span is 2,097,151: parallelism of only 10. Sixteen workers and 64 workers both need at least 2,097,151 steps. Making the merge itself parallel brings the span down to the order of the cube of log n (about 2,871 in the model used here) and makes thousands of workers useful. Parallelising the obvious part is not enough: find the chain that must stay serial.

pros: Turns many problems into a few lines of recursion with a clean cost analysis
Often beats the direct approach by nearly a factor of n: n log n against n squared for sorting
The independent sub-problems map naturally to threads, machines and caches
Small sub-problems fit in the cache, which in practice helps beyond the operation count
cons: The combine step can eat the whole benefit, and it often needs extra memory (merge sort copies)
Recursion costs stack space and call overhead, so small base cases are usually handled directly
The master theorem covers only equal-sized splits and a regular cost function; other shapes need the recursion tree or a more general theorem
Parallel speed-up is limited by the serial combine at the top, not by the number of workers
whenToUse: The problem splits into independent, similar sub-problems that are a constant factor smaller, with a combine step cheaper than solving from scratch
Sorting, searching in ordered data, counting inversions, closest pair, fast multiplication and other well-known divide-and-conquer shapes
Work that should spread across cores or machines, such as map-reduce style aggregation
You need the cost of a recursive algorithm and the recursion tree gives it level by level
whenNotToUse: The sub-problems overlap heavily: memoization or a table avoids the repeated work, as in Fibonacci or edit distance
The split cannot be balanced or removes only a few elements each time: the depth and the cost grow with n
The combine step costs as much as the original problem: the root dominates and the split adds only overhead
The input is tiny: a plain loop or insertion sort has no recursion overhead and is simpler, which is why real libraries switch to it for small pieces
pitfalls: Assuming any split gives n log n: a fixed fraction does (23,121 and 38,125 operations for 1,000 elements), but peeling off one element is quadratic (757,941) and needs a stack frame per element
Applying the master theorem to a recurrence it does not cover: T(n) = T(n - 1) + n subtracts, it does not divide, and splits of unequal size need the recursion tree or a more general result
Forgetting the combine cost: with f(n) = n squared the split saves nothing visible (2,096,128 total, 1,048,576 at the root alone)
Counting the extra memory as free: merge sort copies every element at every level, which is about half of the 18,717 operations here (9,976), and the temporary arrays cost allocation and cache misses
Recursing to a single element: below some size the call overhead costs more than the work, so stop splitting and use a simple method on small pieces
Expecting linear speed-up from more workers: with a sequential final merge the available parallelism is about 10 at 2 to the power 20 elements, so 16 or 64 workers take the same 2,097,151 steps
Spawning a task per recursive call: the cost of scheduling can exceed the work in a small sub-problem. Parallelise only the top levels and cut off below a size threshold

roles.label: Problem
roles.description: The whole input of size n, handed to the top-level call.

roles.label: Splitter
roles.description: Cuts the input into smaller pieces of the same kind.

roles.label: Sub-problems
roles.description: The smaller pieces, each solved by the same method.

roles.label: Combine step
roles.description: Merges the partial answers into the answer for the whole.

roles.label: Workers
roles.description: Threads or machines that can solve independent pieces at the same time.

quiz.question: Splitting a list 10% and 90% instead of 50% and 50% takes merge sort on 1,000 elements from 18,717 to 38,125 operations. What does that show?
options: Only an even split can ever give n log n.
Merge sort becomes quadratic once the split is uneven at all.
The merge step gets slower when the halves differ in size.
A fixed-fraction split keeps the depth logarithmic, so the cost stays n log n with a larger constant.
quiz.explanation: Every piece still shrinks by a constant factor, so there are only about log n levels, at roughly n work each. The depth went from 11 to 59, which is the larger constant. Peeling off one element is different: depth n and quadratic cost.

quiz.question: In T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + n squared, the top level costs 1,048,576 of a total 2,096,128 at n = 1,024. What does that say about the recursion?
options: The leaves dominate, so the total is the number of leaves.
Every level costs the same, so the total is n squared times log n.
The root dominates: the combine step costs about as much as everything below it, so splitting barely helps.
The recurrence has no solution because the combine step is too large.
quiz.explanation: Level costs fall by half at each step down (n squared, then half of it, and so on), so the sum is about twice the top level. A plain algorithm that does the combine work directly would cost about the same.

quiz.question: Merge sort with a sequential final merge has work 22,020,096 and span 2,097,151 at 2 to the power 20 elements. Why do 64 workers not finish sooner than 16?
options: The extra workers spend their time waiting for memory.
Merge sort cannot be run on more than 16 workers.
The final merge is one chain of dependent steps, so no number of workers goes below the span.
Work is divided only among a power of two of the workers, so 64 is rounded down.
quiz.explanation: Time cannot drop below the span, 2,097,151 steps here, however many workers share the rest. Work divided by span is about 10, so around ten workers are the most that can be kept busy until the merge itself is made parallel.
